title: Onmanorama Explains | Is it ethically right for Kerala to use a cheaper generic drug to treat Spinal Muscular Atrophy?
content: On July 5 this year, the Kerala Health and Family Welfare Department decided to procure a considerably cheaper generic formulation of the drug Risdiplam used to treat Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a progressive neuromuscular disorder. Under the KARE (Kerala United Against Rare Disease) programme, the Kerala government has been procuring Risdiplam from Roche, a Swiss healthcare giant, under the brand name Evrysdi. Roche holds the patent for the Risdiplam formulation. The patented drug is called the 'innovator formulation'. The state requires 2133 bottles of Risdiplam annually for the treatment of the existing 109 beneficiaries under the KARE Programme. Each Evrysdi bottle costs 5.2 lakh. However, as part of a deal cut with the Kerala government, Roche provides 11 bottles free for every four bottles procured. Meaning, Kerala has to pay only for 568 bottles. Therefore, instead of 110.92 crore, Kerala has to shell out only 29.54 crore annually. The government purchases the bottles and administers it free of cost to beneficiaries, children up to 12 years, free. Kerala is the only state to provide costly Risdiplam free. In October 2025, the Indian pharmaceutical company Natco Pharma came up with a generic formulation of Risdiplam under the brand name Natsmart. A Natsmart bottle is priced at 15,900 per bottle, just 3 per cent of Roche's cost. At this price, 2133 Risdiplam bottles can be purchased for just 3.39 crore. The price has now been negotiated down to 8500 a bottle. Roche went to court saying that Natco had violated its Indian patent. Though Roche's patent is valid till 2035, the Delhi High Court on October 9 sanctioned the manufacture of Natsmart, and nearly a fortnight ago, on September 30, the Kerala High Court allowed Kerala to proceed with the tender process to procure Risdiplam. Why is Natco's generic drug feared? The underlying fear among parents of SMA-afflicted children is that there is no scientific evidence to show that Natco's generic formulation is efficient and safe. A bioequivalence study, for instance, has not been conducted. A bioequivalence study is done, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO), "to establish the absence of a statistically significant difference in the rate and extent of absorption of an active pharmaceutical ingredient from a pharmaceutical product in comparison with the reference product when administered under similar conditions in an appropriately designed study". In other words, the study is done to check whether the generic drug (Natsmart) has the same effect as the innovator drug (Evrydsi). What is Natco's defence? Natco says a bioequivalence study is not required for Natsmart under WHO guidelines—Multisource (generic) pharmaceutical products: guidelines on registration requirements to establish interchangeability. Clause 4 speaks of instances where equivalence studies are not necessary. Clause 4(b) says that equivalence studies are not required when pharmaceutically equivalent products (Evrydsi and Natsmart) are solutions for oral use (e.g. syrups, elixirs and tinctures), contain the API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) in the same molar concentration as the comparator product (Roche's Evrysdi). Risdiplam is administered in oral dosage form, and both Evrysdi and Natsmart have the same molecule; thus, Natsmart is exempt from equivalence study. Further, Natco has been granted the requisite regulatory approval by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) for the manufacture and marketing of Natsmart as a generic formulation of Risdiplam. Natco also argues that there exists no literature reporting a failure of Natsmart in any patient anywhere nor is there any complaint from any patient, caregiver or treating physician. There is no notice, recall, suspension or adverse finding of the CDSCO either...
